title: Croot's colouring theorem as a 'thick reservoir' template
connection: Croot (Annals 2003) proved every finite colouring of the integers has a monochromatic set with Σ1/n = 1 by finding many smooth-number unit-fraction representations ↔ ES needs one 3-term representation at a prescribed denominator.
why: Croot's engine extracts existence from a thick smooth-number reservoir; listing exactly which step needs freedom of denominators tells us which ES relaxation (e.g. 4/p with k terms, k growing) is in reach.
first_step: Read Croot's proof outline and write down the smallest k(p) for which his method gives 4/p as a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ p^C.
refs: E. Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. of Math. 157 (2003)

title: Bloom's positive-density unit-fraction theorem: what replaces density at one target
connection: Bloom (arXiv:2112.03726) shows any set of positive upper density contains a finite S with Σ_{n∈S}1/n = 1 via Fourier analysis on smooth numbers ↔ ES is a three-term, single-target analogue.
why: Quantifies how many terms Fourier/smooth-number machinery needs; if a bounded-term variant at prescribed numerator 4/p ever fell out, it would be the first such.
first_step: Extract from Bloom's paper the explicit term-count used and check whether any lemma gives representations of a/q with O(1) terms for structured q.

title: Bloom–(shifted primes) unit fractions as a test of 'prescribed-denominator-shape' methods
connection: Bloom's 'Unit fractions with shifted prime denominators' (arXiv:2305.02689) represents 1 with denominators p−1 ↔ ES denominators are constrained to be multiples of p or p-tied.
why: A method that works with arithmetically constrained denominators is closer to ES's constraint than free-denominator results.
first_step: Read 2305.02689 abstract/intro and list which constraint (shifted primes) survived the Fourier argument and why; ask if 'denominators ≡ 0 mod p' is analogous.

title: Sierpiński 5/n and Schinzel m/n conjectures as a uniform family
connection: ES is m = 4 of 'm/n = three unit fractions for n ≥ n_m'; 5/n (Sierpiński) has no known exception ↔ 8/n fails at 131, 241.
why: Any proof for m = 4 must explain why m = 8 fails; studying the transition m = 4,5,6,7 → 8 isolates the numerator-dependent ingredient.
first_step: Tabulate, for m = 4..12, the per-residue-class solution counts at primes ≤ 10⁶ and locate the m where the minimum count first hits 0.

title: Mordell's identities ↔ Rosati/Yamamoto/Aigner tables as an early 'covering system' history
connection: Mordell's mod-840 reduction and later moduli (Yamamoto, Salez's modular filters) form an increasing covering chain ↔ covering-system theory (Erdős, Hough's minimum modulus theorem).
why: Hough proved covering systems with distinct moduli have bounded minimum modulus; ES coverings are of a different type (non-distinct, polynomial classes), and stating precisely why Hough's method doesn't apply is cheap.
first_step: Write the ES modular filters as a 'polynomial covering' and check whether Hough/Balister–Bollobás–Morris–Sahasrabudhe–Tiba distortion method covers polynomial-residue coverings.
refs: R. Hough, Ann. of Math. 181 (2015) — check citation

title: Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy algorithm dynamics on 4/p
connection: Greedy expansion 4/p → 1/⌈p/4⌉ + remainder gives ≤4 terms; ES asks for one fewer ↔ dynamics of the remainder map r/q ↦ (−q mod r)/(q⌈q/r⌉).
why: Greedy produces 3 terms exactly when the second remainder has numerator 1; characterising when 'greedy + one swap' succeeds is a structured sub-question.
first_step: Compute for primes p ≡ 1 (mod 24) ≤ 10⁷ the fraction where greedy-with-one-alternative-first-step gives 3 terms; fit vs log p.

title: Odd greedy algorithm (Stein–Selfridge–Graham) termination problem as a sibling
connection: Whether the odd-denominator greedy algorithm always terminates is open ↔ ES is another 'short Egyptian expansion always exists' statement; both lack an invariant.
why: Techniques developed for one (e.g. 2-adic potential functions) may produce invariants for the other.
first_step: Check current status of odd greedy termination (Guy UPINT D11) and whether any partial result used a monovariant that has an ES analogue.
refs: R. K. Guy, Unsolved Problems in Number Theory, D11

title: Erdős–Graham book 'Old and new problems' chapter on unit fractions as a map of solved/unsolved
connection: Erdős–Graham (1980) list dozens of unit-fraction problems; several since solved (Croot, Bloom, Martin) ↔ ES.
why: Each solved neighbour gives a method; an indexed table 'problem → method → why it fails for ES' extends the z52 dossier cheaply.
first_step: Pull every unit-fraction problem from erdosproblems.com with status 'proved' and record the key method in one line each.

title: Martin's dense Egyptian fractions and the 'many representations' regime
connection: Greg Martin showed every rational has Egyptian representations with denominators of positive density in [1,N]-ish ranges ↔ ES wants sparse (3-term) ones.
why: The interpolation between dense and 3-term representations (k-term for k slowly growing) is a ladder whose rungs could be climbed down one at a time.
first_step: Check whether 'every 4/p is a sum of k unit fractions with denominators ≤ p^A' is known for k = 4 with explicit A (yes trivially?) and find the least k proved with denominators ≤ C·p.

title: Four unit fractions are easy: why 4/p = four terms is trivial and what the 4→3 step loses
connection: 4/p = 1/x1+…+1/x4 always solvable (e.g. via greedy) ↔ ES 3 terms; the 4-term solution set is a 'thick object' and ES asks it to degenerate.
why: A collapse map from 4-term to 3-term solutions (merging two fractions with sum a unit fraction) is an extraction rule in the G1 sense.
first_step: Count 4-term solutions with two terms summing to a unit fraction; check whether that count is ≍ the 3-term count or larger (identity check).

title: Tao's 2011 blog post comment thread as a mine of unexplored ideas
connection: Tao's blog post on the Elsholtz–Tao paper drew comments with heuristic and computational ideas ↔ campaign may not have harvested all.
why: Cheap source of community-generated angles that were never followed up.
first_step: Read the comments on terrytao.wordpress.com 2011/07 'On the number of solutions to 4/p = …' and extract each distinct idea into this list.

title: Webb's density theorem and Li Delang's improvement as historical sieve calibration
connection: Webb (1970) and Li (1981) bounded the exceptional set with large sieve ↔ campaign's exp(−c(log N)^{3/4}) bound.
why: Comparing exponents across history shows the speed of sieve improvement; extrapolating suggests whether 'exceptional set finite' is near any sieve horizon.
first_step: Tabulate historical exceptional-set bounds (Webb, Vaughan, Li, campaign) with year and method in a 6-row table.

title: Graham's 1964 theorem: which rationals are sums of reciprocals of distinct squares
connection: Graham characterised rationals representable by finite sums of distinct reciprocal squares (finite exception list) ↔ ES-type 'all but finitely many / all' statements.
why: A proved 'every rational in a range except finitely many structured exceptions' theorem for unit fractions is a structural precedent like U(n)'s six sporadics.
first_step: Read Graham, 'On finite sums of reciprocals of distinct nth powers' (Pacific J. Math 1964) and note whether its method uses a thick reservoir (likely yes).
refs: R. L. Graham, Pacific J. Math. 14 (1964) — verify

title: Sylvester's sequence and the extremal 1 = Σ1/x_i problem as a dual
connection: Sylvester's sequence gives extremal denominators in Σ1/x_i = 1 ↔ ES's largest denominator is bounded by p²·(…); extremal structure constrains solution shape.
why: Bounding the largest denominator in any ES solution (Curtiss/Soundararajan-type bounds) restricts the search space and may give a finite-check argument shape.
first_step: Compute max(z)/p² over all ES solutions for primes ≤ 10⁵ and compare to Curtiss-type extremal bounds.

title: Znám's problem / Giuga numbers as Egyptian-fraction divisibility siblings
connection: Znám's problem (x_i | Πx_j + 1) and Giuga numbers (Σ1/p − Π1/p ∈ ℤ) are unit-fraction divisibility conditions solved by computer + structure ↔ ES Type II divisibility d | 4Cp+1.
why: Shows how divisibility-with-unit-fractions problems were attacked; may suggest a structural descent.
first_step: Write the ES Type II condition in Znám form (product of denominators ≡ ±1 mod each) and compare.

title: Erdős–Straus for polynomial rings: transfer the F_q[T] proof's structure
connection: ES over F_q[T] has proved variants ↔ integers; the function-field proof uses degree as an additive height and polynomial factorisation freedom.
why: Locating exactly which F_q[T] step uses 'degree additivity' or 'many irreducibles of each degree' tells what integer input is missing.
first_step: Re-read the repo's F_q[T] treatment and annotate each step by which property of F_q[T] it uses (Riemann hypothesis for curves? degree splitting?).

title: Erdős–Straus over number fields (Gaussian, Eisenstein) with sign/positivity conditions
connection: Generalise ES to totally positive elements in totally real fields ↔ ℤ[√2], ℚ(√5).
why: In ℚ(√5) the unit group is infinite and positive; the existence of units might act as a thick reservoir that ℤ lacks, giving a proved sibling.
first_step: Brute-force 4/π = sum of three totally positive unit-reciprocals for small totally positive primes π of ℤ[(1+√5)/2]; check for failures.

title: Elsholtz's k-term results: sums of k unit fractions with k ≥ 4 and m/n
connection: Elsholtz (Trans. AMS 2001) 'Sums of k unit fractions' gives lower bounds on solution counts for m/n with k terms ↔ ES k = 3.
why: The k = 4 exceptional set may be provably empty for fixed m with large n by thick-reservoir arguments; seeing why k=3 is not reachable sharpens the barrier.
first_step: Check whether 'm/n = sum of 4 unit fractions for all large n' is proved for each fixed m (and which method), via Elsholtz 2001.

title: Vaughan's proof as a fixed point: re-derive with modern large-sieve inequalities
connection: Vaughan 1970 used the large sieve ↔ modern variants (Iwaniec's bilinear, multiplicative large sieve for sparse moduli, Baier–Zhao for square moduli).
why: Campaign has 3/4 exponent; large sieve for moduli of special form (e.g. 4uB) may give a different exponent shape.
first_step: Check whether a large sieve for moduli in the multiplicative semigroup {4uB} (product moduli) exists in literature (search 'large sieve product moduli').

title: The unit-fraction 'Erdős–Graham r/s with denominators in a set' (Erdős #, Bleicher) problem
connection: Which rationals have representations using denominators from a prescribed set ↔ ES: denominators from the p-tied set.
why: Treating ES as representability over a structured denominator set imports matroid/semigroup tools.
first_step: Search erdosproblems.com for problems about 'denominators from a set A' and list status.

title: Lagrange four squares → three squares (Legendre/Gauss) as the classic local-global fixed-length analogue
connection: Three squares represent n iff n ≠ 4^a(8b+7), proved via genus theory/ternary forms ↔ ES ternary 'rational' form with no local obstruction.
why: Three squares is a fixed-length, every-n theorem with a power-size count (√n class number); contrasting with ES's polylog count is the barrier. Still a useful 'how was it proved' row.
first_step: Write down the Gauss three-squares proof as thick object (class group) × extraction rule (genus) and fit it into the G1 matrix.

title: Duke's equidistribution of CM points as the analytic proof of 'every large n' for ternary forms
connection: Duke–Iwaniec–Schulze-Pillot: every sufficiently large n locally represented by a ternary form in its spinor genus is represented ↔ ES's ternary surface.
why: ES is a cubic not quadratic, but the Type II slice reduces to binary/ternary quadratic questions for fixed C; ternary forms with growing discriminant are the closest proved analogues.
first_step: Identify whether any ES slice at prime p is a ternary quadratic representation problem with discriminant bounded independent of p.

title: Ramanujan's 1/x+1/y+1/z representation of the form x²+y²+10z² anecdote: 'almost all but unknown exceptions' history
connection: Ramanujan's ternary form x²+y²+10z² represents all odd n except a finite unknown list (Ono–Soundararajan under GRH) ↔ ES conditional finite-exception results.
why: A conditional (GRH) 'finitely many exceptions, explicitly bounded' result for a thin-ish problem; template for a GRH-conditional ES-adjacent theorem.
first_step: Read Ono–Soundararajan (Invent. 1997) structure: they need GRH for an L-function lower bound (Siegel-zero avoidance); ask what L-function ES would need.
refs: K. Ono, K. Soundararajan, Invent. Math. 130 (1997) — verify

title: Goldbach-type ternary (Vinogradov/Helfgott) as 'every n, power count' calibration
connection: Helfgott proved ternary Goldbach for all odd n > 5 by combining asymptotic and verification to 10^27-ish ↔ ES verified to 10^18 but no asymptotic.
why: Helfgott's split (explicit asymptotic beyond C, computation below) is the template if ES ever got an explicit-constant theorem; the campaign could ask what explicit constant a conditional ES-adjacent theorem would need.
first_step: Write down which explicit lower bound for R(p) (vs log² p) would, combined with 10¹⁸ verification, suffice; record as a 'Helfgott target'.

title: Catalan/Mihăilescu as an 'algebraic rigidity' row: cyclotomic arguments solved a polylog-sparse problem
connection: Mihăilescu's proof uses cyclotomic units and Stickelberger annihilators ↔ ES: is there a cyclotomic field attached to p where a certificate must exist?
why: Rigidity (R) is one of two sources for thin pointwise theorems; Catalan is a canonical (R) instance worth mapping.
first_step: Attempt: attach to p the field ℚ(ζ_p) or ℚ(√p) and ask whether ES(p) failing implies a nontrivial relation in its class group / unit group.

title: Fermat's two-squares via Zagier's one-sentence involution and its ES analogue
connection: Zagier's involution on {x²+4yz=p} has one fixed point so the other involution has one too ↔ ES windmills (INVOLUTION_ES2).
why: Already studied; remains the canonical (T)×parity cell. Listing for completeness and to try non-affine menus.
first_step: Enumerate solutions of 4/p in some normalised parametrisation and look for any involution whose fixed-point count is odd for all p ≤ 10⁵.

title: Heath-Brown's count of rational points on Cayley's cubic surface (1/x0+…+1/x3 = 0)
connection: 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ 1/x+1/y+1/z+1/(−n/4)=0 places ES points on Cayley's 4-nodal cubic with one coordinate prescribed ↔ Heath-Brown (math/0210333) counts its rational points (order B (log B)^6).
why: A fibration of the Cayley cubic by the value of one coordinate turns ES into 'every fibre has an integral point'; Manin-conjecture machinery for this surface is known.
first_step: Read math/0210333 and check whether the universal torsor parametrisation it uses restricts nicely to fibres with x3 = −n/4 (or n·t).

title: Saturation number of Cayley's cubic (arXiv:1406.6963) as an almost-prime ES variant
connection: Saturation results show points on Cayley's cubic with coordinates having few prime factors ↔ ES coordinates have p-adic constraints.
why: If one can force coordinates with bounded Ω on Cayley's cubic, the ES fibre version with one coordinate p·t might be a sieve-reachable relaxation.
first_step: Read 1406.6963 abstract; ask whether its method yields points with a coordinate in a prescribed class mod p.

title: Markoff triples (Bourgain–Gamburd–Sarnak, Chen) as 'orbit forces divisibility' precedent
connection: Chen proved every Markoff orbit mod p has size ≡ 0 mod p ↔ ES lacks a group action; Cayley cubic does have Markoff-like Vieta moves (1/x0+… = 0 is Cremona-symmetric).
why: The Cayley cubic has a large birational automorphism group (Cremona involutions x_i ↦ 1/x_i pattern); an action on ES fibres would be new structure.
first_step: Compute the birational automorphisms of the surface 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n preserving the fibre; check for non-permutation Vieta-like involutions (e.g. quadratic in one variable).

title: Kloosterman/Linnik's ternary problem x²+y²+z²=n history as dual of Type II divisor question
connection: Linnik's ergodic method proved equidistribution of representations of n by sums of three squares under a splitting condition ↔ ES divisor equidistribution at one integer.
why: Linnik's ergodic method gives pointwise results with an auxiliary-prime splitting condition; ES with an auxiliary splitting condition (e.g. 'if some small prime ℓ splits in ℚ(√−p)…') is a conditional sibling.
first_step: Formulate 'ES(p) holds when (ℓ/p)=1 for some fixed small ℓ' via Linnik-style equidistribution and see which object would need to equidistribute.

title: Ellenberg–Venkatesh 'local-global for representations of quadratic forms by forms' as pointwise via ergodic theory
connection: EV proved local-global for representations of a quadratic form by another with an auxiliary splitting prime ↔ ES fibre as 'representation of p by a cubic form family'.
why: Precedent for pointwise results via unipotent dynamics; a Ratner-type input on an ES-associated homogeneous space would be new.
first_step: Check whether ES Type II slice (4uBC − u − B = p) is an orbit-counting problem on a homogeneous space SL₂(ℝ)×… (it is affine in C — maybe).

title: The 'Egyptian fractions with prime denominators' problem (Erdős–Graham) and ES with prime z
connection: Sums of reciprocals of primes equal to 1/n or rationals ↔ ES solutions where denominators are constrained.
why: Constrained-denominator versions sharpen intuition about which constraints are free.
first_step: Count ES solutions of 4/p where y/p or z/p is prime; check whether always ≥1 to 10⁶ (a strengthening that could fail early).

title: Swett / Mihnea–Dumitru verification algorithms as history of computational ES
connection: Verification to 10^17 (Salez) and 10^18 (Mihnea–Dumitru preprint) uses modular sieving ↔ structural information embedded in which filters remove which primes.
why: The residual set after filters is the computational 'hard core'; its structure (which modular filters never suffice) is data for a theorem.
first_step: Read arXiv:2509.00128 and record the final residue-class filter set and the fraction of primes needing brute force.

title: Rav, Schinzel–Sierpiński polynomial identities (no identity for square classes) as a Galois-theoretic obstruction
connection: Mordell–Schinzel: no polynomial identity solves ES on a residue class containing squares ↔ Galois/monodromy of the solution variety over ℚ(n).
why: The obstruction is 'no rational section'; asking for multi-sections of bounded degree or sections over ℚ(√n) or ℚ(n^{1/k}) is a natural relaxation.
first_step: Search for algebraic (non-polynomial) identities: solutions x(n),y(n),z(n) ∈ ℚ(√n) or ℚ(√(n+c)) that specialise to integers for many n.

title: Ellipsoid-type 'every integer is a sum of three cubes?' (Booker–Sutherland) as a computation-driven sibling
connection: Three cubes: thin count, no local obstruction for n ≢ ±4 mod 9, open; computational breakthroughs via Elkies-type lattice methods ↔ ES.
why: Same calibration class (thin count, open); their algorithmic ideas (Elkies' lattice reduction for small cubic values) may port to ES search.
first_step: Read Booker 'Cracking the problem with 33' and check whether its algorithm adapts to finding ES solutions with huge denominators for adversarial p.

title: Two-stage ES tree with Huang–Vaughan binary statistics at the second stage
connection: Generic form: write 4/p as a sum of two fractions each with numerator 1 or 2 in a specific way ↔ ES via 4/p = 1/x + 3/(px')…
why: Splits ES into a two-step tree; each step is binary Egyptian (well-understood: Huang–Vaughan counts).
first_step: Enumerate decompositions 4/p = 1/x + r/s with r/s a 2-term-representable fraction and compare count distribution with Huang–Vaughan binary statistics.

title: Binary Egyptian fractions: m/n = 1/x + 1/y criterion (Rav) as building block
connection: m/n = 1/x+1/y iff there exist divisors d1,d2 of n with m | d1+d2 ↔ ES = choose first term then binary criterion.
why: Rav's criterion turns ES into: ∃x, (4x−p)/(px) binary-representable ⟺ divisor-sum condition; a clean finite search per x.
first_step: Implement ES via 'x then Rav criterion' and compute the smallest successful x per prime ≤ 10⁸; compare its growth with log p.

title: Ahmadi–Bleicher and 'exceptional set has measure zero' line as an independent history thread
connection: Several 1990s–2000s results counted ES solution sets on average ↔ ET 2013.
why: Cheap literature completeness check; may contain a technique (e.g. Bleicher's construction) the campaign lacks.
first_step: Search MathSciNet/zbMATH for 'Erdős–Straus' 1990–2010 and list techniques per paper.

title: Hilbert's tenth problem lens: is 'ES for all n' Π₁ and could it be independent?
connection: ES is a Π₂ statement naively (∀n∃xyz) but with a computable bound on x,y,z (z ≤ n²·…) it is Π₁ ↔ Gödel/Matiyasevich.
why: Π₁ statements are either true or refutable by a finite counterexample; recording this frames 'unprovable but true' as the only independence scenario.
first_step: Write down the explicit bound making ES a bounded-quantifier statement and note its consequence (any proof exists in a sufficiently strong theory iff true and provable).

title: Sum-of-two-squares for primes in thin sequences (Friedlander–Iwaniec x²+y⁴) as 'thin but proven' calibration
connection: FI proved infinitely many primes x²+y⁴ via bilinear forms ↔ ES needs every p, not infinitely many; still calibrates bilinear technology on thin sets.
why: Bilinear structure in ES (R(p) as sum over (u,C) pairs) may allow a Type I/II sieve split for averaged statements in thin p-sets.
first_step: Check: does R(p) averaged over primes in a thin sequence (e.g. p = x²+y⁴) admit FI's bilinear decomposition? Write the sum.

title: Erdős's 1950 paper 'Az 1/x1+…+1/xn = a/b egyenlet egész számú megoldásairól' original motivation
connection: Original Hungarian paper where ES appears ↔ what Erdős believed the method should be.
why: Historical intent sometimes contains a suggested approach never followed up.
first_step: Locate a translation or summary of Erdős 1950 (Mat. Lapok 1) and record Erdős's own heuristic.

title: Straus's contributions and correspondence
connection: Ernst Straus co-posed ES; his other work (Straus on Egyptian fractions, Erdős–Straus irrationality series) ↔ ES.
why: Irrationality criteria for Σ1/a_n (Erdős–Straus) use similar unit-fraction growth arguments; maybe a dynamical link.
first_step: Check Straus's papers list for any ES partial result or heuristic.

title: Guy's UPINT D11 bibliography completeness sweep
connection: UPINT D11 lists references on ES and related unit-fraction problems ↔ repo LITERATURE_2026.md.
why: Cross-checking a canonical bibliography against the repo's literature file is cheap and catches missed classics.
first_step: Get UPINT D11 references and diff with LITERATURE_2026.md.

title: Breusch/Stewart: rationals with odd denominator have odd-denominator Egyptian expansions
connection: Breusch–Stewart theorem (any r/s, s odd, is a finite sum of distinct odd unit fractions) proved by a constructive argument ↔ ES with parity-constrained denominators.
why: Parity constraints on denominators are a natural ES strengthening; its proof technique may hint at constructive arguments.
first_step: Compute: for primes p ≤ 10⁶, does 4/p always have a 3-term solution with all denominators odd? (Certainly not when … check quickly.)

title: ES with distinct denominators vs. allowing repeats — trivial reductions sanity table
connection: ES allows x=y; distinct version is equivalent for large n? ↔ known small cases.
why: Cheap sanity: if distinct ES fails at some p while ES holds, that's a data point about solution-set rigidity.
first_step: Compute primes ≤ 10⁷ where all solutions have a repeated denominator (expect none beyond tiny p).

title: Erdős–Graham 'bound on the number of solutions' (Browning–Elsholtz upper bounds) as a structural pressure
connection: Browning–Elsholtz bounded the number of solutions of m/n Egyptian 3-term equations from above ↔ lower bound needed.
why: Upper-bound techniques (divisor bounds on a determinantal parametrisation) give the parametrisation used for lower bounds too.
first_step: Read Browning–Elsholtz 'The number of representations of rationals as a sum of unit fractions' (Illinois J. Math. 2011?) and extract its parametrisation.

title: Conway's 'topograph' viewpoint on binary forms → ES Type II as walk on topograph
connection: Type II involves binary quadratic data (4uB − 1 · …) ↔ Conway's topograph gives a tree-walk picture of representations.
why: Topograph rivers/climbing lemma give constructive representation existence for indefinite forms; might give a constructive certificate walk.
first_step: Express 4uBC − u − B = p with C fixed as a binary form representation and draw its topograph for p = 409 (a (★)-failure).

title: Moree/Pomerance–Weingartner on m/n exceptions as numerator-uniform calibration
connection: Pomerance–Weingartner study the m/n three-unit-fraction exceptions ↔ ES m=4; their density heuristic for exceptions as m grows.
why: Their exception-generation mechanism (n in specific residue classes making all slices fail) is exactly what ES must avoid; reading why it can't occur for m=4 is a structural lemma target.
first_step: Extract PW's mechanism for exceptions at m=8 (n=131, 241) and test whether a 'virtual' m=4 version exists at some modulus.

title: Dirichlet series of ES solution counts and multiple-zeta-like structure
connection: Multiple zeta values have Egyptian-fraction-flavoured sum structure ↔ generating functions of ES solution counts.
why: Generating function Σ_n f(n) n^{-s} for ES counts may be expressible via double/triple Dirichlet series with MZV-like structure.
first_step: Check whether a paper on Dirichlet series Σ f(n)n^{-s} of Egyptian counts exists (search 'Dirichlet series number of Egyptian fraction representations').

title: Hensel-lifting history: 'every n locally' proof as a template audit
connection: Local solubility of ES at every prime is easy ↔ global fails only by non-BM obstruction; history of local-global for cubic surfaces (Swinnerton-Dyer, Colliot-Thélène) applies to rational not integral points.
why: Integral Hasse principle on log K3 / log Fano surfaces is where ES sits; recent work (Harpaz, Wilsch) on integral points of log Fano varieties gives counts on average.
first_step: Check Wilsch's thesis/papers on 'integral points of bounded height on log Fano threefolds' for anything about 1/x+1/y+1/z-type surfaces.

title: Unit-fraction Tilings: Egyptian squares (Rédei-style tiling by rectangles of area 1/n)
connection: Tiling a rectangle by rectangles of sides 1/a×1/b relates to Egyptian decompositions ↔ ES as a 3-piece tiling of a 4×p-ish rectangle.
why: Tilings give geometric invariants (Dehn-type) that sometimes prove impossibility or existence.
first_step: Formulate: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ tiling of a (4·lcm)-strip; check if any Dehn-like invariant is non-trivial.

title: Universal torsor of the ES surface and its integral points
connection: The ES surface U_n is a (log) del Pezzo/ toric-type surface; universal torsors linearise counting (Salberger, Heath-Brown) ↔ Type I/II parametrisations are torsor coordinates.
why: If the ET parametrisations are exactly the universal torsor, then ES(p) ⟺ an integral point on an affine variety with a free torus action — and the variety might have extra structure (e.g. be a cone over a known variety).
first_step: Compute Pic of a smooth compactification of U_n and compare the ET variables (a,b,c,d,e,f) with Cox ring generators.

title: Cox ring of the minimal resolution of the Cayley cubic, fibred over n
connection: The Cayley cubic's Cox ring is known explicitly (Derenthal et al. list Cox rings of singular del Pezzo surfaces) ↔ ES fibre is a hyperplane section x3 = const·n.
why: Explicit Cox ring coordinates for this family would give the 'right' variables in which ES might become a norm or divisor problem with new symmetry.
first_step: Look up Derenthal 'Singular del Pezzo surfaces whose universal torsors are hypersurfaces' and identify Cayley's cubic (4A1) entry.

title: Integral points on log K3 surfaces: Harpaz's results as framework
connection: Harpaz proved results on integral points on log K3 surfaces (e.g. complements of hyperplane triangles) ↔ U_n = P² minus a cubic-ish divisor? classify (U_n's log type).
why: Knowing U_n's log Kodaira dimension places ES among 'expected Hasse principle' or 'expected failures' classes.
first_step: Compute log Kodaira dimension of U_n (complement of the boundary divisor xyz = 0 in the cubic surface) and check against Harpaz's log K3 framework.

title: Strong approximation failure beyond Brauer–Manin: étale-Brauer / descent obstructions for U_n integral points
connection: BL show BM does not explain all failures of strong approximation for U_n ↔ étale-Brauer or descent obstruction might.
why: A computable finer obstruction set would refine which integral 'adelic' points lift; if it is empty at primes, that would be a structural non-obstruction theorem.
first_step: List finite étale covers of U_n (fundamental group of complement) of small degree and test whether their twists have integral points at failing (★)-primes like 409.

title: Fundamental group of the complement of the ES boundary and Kummer covers
connection: U_n's boundary consists of lines/conics; π₁ of complement gives covers ↔ Type I/II divisibility conditions may be torsor conditions under μ_k.
why: Interpreting d | 4Cp+1, d ≡ −1 mod 4C as a μ_{4C}-torsor condition would explain the tied modulus geometrically.
first_step: Compute H¹_et(U_n, μ_m) for small m via the boundary configuration and match classes with the ET congruence conditions.

title: Thin sets in Serre's sense: is the set of n with ES(n) failing contained in a thin set?
connection: Hilbert irreducibility / thin sets ↔ a counterexample set to a fibration's integral-point existence often lies in a thin set.
why: If ES-failures were forced into a thin set (values of a finite cover), combining with Dickson-type heuristics might bound them.
first_step: Test numerically whether hard (★)-failure primes (409, …, 8813281) are values of a low-degree polynomial or norm form more often than random.

title: Fibration method (Colliot-Thélène–Harpaz–Wittenberg) for integral points on families over A¹_n
connection: The total space {4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)} ⊂ A⁴ fibred over n ↔ fibration method proves Hasse principle for 'almost all fibres' under Schinzel's hypothesis.
why: A Schinzel-conditional statement 'ES for all n in a set of density 1 among primes with explicit exceptions' via fibration method would be new form even if conditional.
first_step: Check if the fibration method has an integral-points version (Harpaz–Wittenberg 'Zero-cycles…'; 'integral fibration method') applicable to cubic fibres.

title: Elliptic fibrations of the ES surface: for fixed x, (y,z) lie on a conic; for fixed ratio, on an elliptic curve?
connection: Slicing U_n by x = const gives a hyperbola (binary divisor problem); slicing by y/z = const gives curves of genus ? ↔ elliptic fibration may give rank-based infinitude.
why: If some pencil of curves on U_n has genus-1 fibres with positive rank uniformly, integral points might be forced via descent heights.
first_step: Compute the genus of the curves cut by y = t·z on the ES projective surface and check if any pencil is elliptic.

title: Rational curves on the ES surface over ℚ(n): degree-d rational families
connection: Polynomial identities = rational curves defined over ℚ(n) on the generic fibre ↔ Mordell–Schinzel says none of low degree for square classes.
why: Counting rational curves of degree d on the generic fibre (Gromov–Witten-ish) and their fields of definition may show a Galois obstruction growing with d.
first_step: For the generic fibre over ℚ(n), compute lines/conics defined over ℚ̄(n) and their Galois orbits.

title: Mordell–Weil-style descent on the 'pencil' S_{n,k} and specialisation k→0
connection: z52 G2 pencil S_{n,k} ↔ Silverman specialisation theorem for families of varieties over the k-line.
why: Specialisation of Brauer groups/Picard ranks along k may detect whether k=0 is a 'jump' fibre.
first_step: Compute the geometric Picard rank of S_{n,k} for generic k vs k=0 (Magma/Sage) and record jumps.

title: Néron–Severi lattice of the ES surface and lattice-theoretic obstructions
connection: NS lattice of a minimal resolution ↔ integral points via intersection pairing constraints.
why: An arithmetic invariant from NS (e.g. discriminant group twisted by n) might be the hidden 'prime T1' carrier.
first_step: Compute NS of the resolved projective closure of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx)w (with w homogenising) and its Galois action as a function of n.

title: Arithmetic of the singular points: the Cayley cubic's four A1 nodes and local data at n
connection: Integral points near nodes correspond to small denominators ↔ local conditions at nodes might be where p's arithmetic enters.
why: Blow-up at nodes introduces exceptional curves; integral points meeting them encode divisibility by p.
first_step: Locate nodes of the ES projective surface for given n and compute which Type I/II solutions reduce mod p to a node.

title: Reduction mod p of the ES surface at n = p: counting F_p-points with constraints
connection: U_p mod p degenerates (n ≡ 0) ↔ solutions for 4/p have p | some denominator; the mod-p geometry of the degenerate fibre controls Type I/II.
why: The degenerate fibre xyz = 0 mod p structure is exactly Type I vs Type II split; higher p-adic structure might give Hensel-type existence.
first_step: Write the p-adic Newton polygon / blow-up of U_n at n = 0 and see whether ES(p) is a statement about ℤ_p-points of a model plus a global condition.

title: Shimura curve / quaternion order reformulation: ES as an embedding problem
connection: Repo knows quaternion-order forms ↔ optimal embeddings counted by class numbers (Eichler); a pointwise embedding existence theorem for orders of growing level.
why: Eichler's embedding theorem gives existence when class number is 1 or via spinor genus; if ES were 'an embedding into a level-p order of a fixed-discriminant ring', existence could be automatic.
first_step: Re-read the repo's quaternion form and determine whether the discriminant of the embedded order is bounded (good) or grows with p (bad).

title: Hecke eigenvalues at p as a certificate source (trace formula identity)
connection: R(p) = trace of some Hecke-like operator? If R(p) = Σ over a set of a_f(p) with f in a fixed space, Deligne's bound would control it.
why: A finite-dimensional space would give R(p) = main + O(p^{1/2-ish}·dim) error — but main is log², so need dim growth; still worth seeing if R(p) has any modular generating function.
first_step: Compute Σ_p R(p) q^p partial sums? Rather: test whether p ↦ R(p) − M(p) correlates with a_f(p) for small-level newforms over primes ≤ 10⁶.

title: Theta series of the ES 'certificate lattice' and its Eisenstein/cusp split
connection: Repo has theta quotients ↔ Siegel–Weil: the Eisenstein part is the genus average; the cusp part is the fluctuation.
why: For ternary forms the cusp part at prime index is bounded by Duke's subconvexity; for ES-type objects identifying the 'weight' and 'level' tells whether subconvexity could ever beat the main term.
first_step: Write R(p) as Fourier coefficient of a (possibly mock / indefinite) theta series; identify weight and level growth.

title: Indefinite theta functions (Zwegers) for counting 4uBC − u − B = p
connection: R(p) counts representations by an indefinite cubic-ish form over a cone ↔ Zwegers/Vignéras indefinite theta series give modularity for cone-restricted counts of quadratic forms.
why: Fix C: 4uBC − u − B is a binary quadratic form in (u,B) (indefinite) plus linear; cone-restricted representation counts have mock modular generating functions.
first_step: For fixed C, write the generating function Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{4CuB−u−B} and test whether it is a known mock theta / Appell–Lerch sum.

title: Appell–Lerch sums: Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{4CuB−u−B} as a Lambert-type series
connection: Σ_{u,B≥1} q^{auB−u−B} = Σ_u q^{−u} q^{(au−1)}/(1−q^{au−1}) is a Lambert/Appell–Lerch series ↔ R(p) is the q^p coefficient of Σ_C of these.
why: Lambert series coefficients are divisor sums; Appell–Lerch sums have modular completions which yield exact formulas for coefficients in some cases.
first_step: Compute the series F(q) = Σ_{C≥1} Σ_{u≥1} q^{4Cu−u−1}/(1−q^{4Cu−1})-type expansion and check against R(n) to 10⁴.

title: Rademacher-type exact formula for a mock modular generating function of R(n)
connection: If Σ R(n) q^n (or a twist) were mock modular, Bringmann–Ono-style exact formulas give coefficients as convergent Kloosterman–Bessel series.
why: Exact formulas with positive main term and explicitly bounded tails are how partition-function positivity facts are proved pointwise.
first_step: Check growth: R(n) is polylog, inconsistent with the exponential growth of weight-<0 mock forms; so look for weight-1 or weight-0 objects (logarithmic growth plausible for weight 1 Eisenstein-like). Test whether n ↦ M₀(n) matches a weight-1 Eisenstein coefficient shape.

title: Weight-1 forms and Kronecker characters: M_BM as a sum of class numbers
connection: M_BM(p) = Σ (1 − χ_{−4uB}(p))/φ(4uB) is an average of characters ↔ L(1,χ) and class numbers of ℚ(√−uB·p)?
why: Swapping sum order may give M_BM(p) as a weighted sum of L-values attached to p; class-number lower bounds (Siegel, Goldfeld) are pointwise.
first_step: Rewrite T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) by grouping by m = uB: Σ_m (−m/p)·g(m) with g(m) = #{splittings}/φ(4m); compare with L(1, (−·/p))-weighted sums.

title: Goldfeld–Gross–Zagier effective class numbers as a pointwise lower-bound precedent
connection: GGZ gave an effective lower bound h(−D) ≫ log D via an elliptic curve of rank 3 ↔ ES needs a pointwise polylog lower bound.
why: One of the very few pointwise lower bounds of logarithmic size in number theory; obtained via an auxiliary L-function with high-order zero. Could ES's count be forced positive by an auxiliary object with forced vanishing?
first_step: Write the abstract structure: positivity of a quantity via an auxiliary L-function's central vanishing; ask what L-function would encode R(p).

title: Class number of ℚ(√−p) and ES: correlation test
connection: h(−4p) controls representations of p by binary forms of discriminant −4p ↔ ES solutions involve binary forms 4uB·…
why: If R(p) correlates with h(−4p) or h(4p)·log ε_p, a class-number formula identity might lurk.
first_step: Compute Pearson/Spearman correlation of R(p)/log²p with h(−4p)/√p and with L(1, χ_p) over primes ≤ 10⁷.

title: Real quadratic fields ℚ(√p): fundamental unit, continued fraction of √p and ES
connection: ES₅ uses continued-fraction length ≤ 3 of something tied to p ↔ the CF of √p (period, palindromes) encodes ℚ(√p) arithmetic.
why: If certificate CFs relate to the CF expansion of √p or (√p+1)/2, the infinite unit group could be a thick reservoir.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵, compare the period of √p with the structure of the smallest ES₅ certificate words.

title: Cluster algebras / friezes: ES₅ words as Conway–Coxeter frieze entries
connection: Repo connects to friezes ↔ SL₂-tilings and friezes with entries tied to p; Conway–Coxeter positivity (Laurent phenomenon) gives positivity for free.
why: Laurent positivity is an exact algebraic positivity source (R-type).
first_step: Search for a frieze pattern of width ≤ 3 whose quiddity contains p-tied entries and whose positivity is ES₅.

title: Tropicalisation of the ES equation and valuations at p
connection: Tropical variety of 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) under p-adic valuation ↔ which valuation patterns (v_p(x),v_p(y),v_p(z)) are allowed (Type I/II).
why: Tropical geometry classifies degenerations; may reveal hidden Type III-ish patterns for composite n and their absence for primes.
first_step: Compute the tropical variety for v_p(n) = 1 and list cones; match with Type I/II.

title: Toric degenerations and Ehrhart counting of ES solutions in boxes
connection: Counting lattice points in polytopes defined by Type II inequalities ↔ Ehrhart quasi-polynomials.
why: The (★) count over a cut-off region is a lattice-point count in a hyperbolic region; Ehrhart theory with dilation p might give exact periodic formulas for partial counts.
first_step: Restrict to u ≤ U, B ≤ V and count solutions mod 4uB to p as function of p; check if it's a quasi-polynomial in p of bounded period.

title: Additive combinatorics: sum-product phenomena in (ℤ/p)^× and ES Type I
connection: Type I: f | p²+4c²d, f ≡ −p mod 4cd ↔ product sets {ab⁻¹ : ab | N} hitting −1 mod e.
why: Sum-product/Bourgain–Glibichuk–Konyagin: product sets of moderate size in (ℤ/q)^× cover everything; e-slice form needs the divisor-ratio set mod e to contain −1.
first_step: For the e-slice form, measure |{ab⁻¹ mod e : ab | N}| / e as function of e for hard primes; check whether it is large enough for generic covering results.

title: Davenport constant / zero-sum theory: a divisor product hitting −1 mod e
connection: Hitting −1 in (ℤ/e)^× by a sub-product of the prime factors of N ↔ zero-sum (Davenport constant) theory: any sequence of length ≥ D(G) has a zero-sum subsequence.
why: If N has ≥ D((ℤ/e)^×) prime factors in suitable classes, a subproduct hits any target in a subgroup — gives existence when Ω(N) is large.
first_step: For hard primes, compute Ω((p+e)/4) vs D((ℤ/e)^×) for small e; count e where Ω exceeds the Davenport bound.

title: Olson's theorem / Erdős–Ginzburg–Ziv for products of divisors
connection: EGZ-type results guarantee subproducts in a coset ↔ ES gate: divisors of N in class −1 mod 4C.
why: Covering targets in multiplicative groups by subproducts is a mature field; ES's issue is target specificity (−1, not identity).
first_step: Restate ES gate as: −1 ∈ Σ*(S) where S = multiset of prime factors of 4Cp+1 in (ℤ/4C)^×; tabulate how often Σ*(S) is the whole group.

title: Sidon/B_h sets: are ES solution denominators 'too structured' to avoid?
connection: Sets avoiding solutions to 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n-type linear-in-reciprocals equations ↔ Ruzsa's theory of sets without solutions of linear equations.
why: Ruzsa-type extremal results for reciprocal equations might give: the set of 'certificate parameters' is too large to avoid the ES hyperplane.
first_step: Search literature: 'sets without solutions to 1/x + 1/y = 1/z' density (Erdős problem) — record what's known.

title: Szemerédi–Trotter / incidence bounds on the modular hyperbola
connection: Solutions (u,B) with 4uB ≡ … are points on modular hyperbolas ↔ incidence geometry over F_p (Bourgain–Katz–Tao, Rudnev) gives lower bounds on structured point sets.
why: Incidence bounds are rigid combinatorial inputs that work pointwise at prime modulus.
first_step: Express ES(p) as existence of an incidence between a point set P_p and a line set L_p over F_p (or ℤ) and check sizes vs Rudnev's bound regime.

title: Polynomial method (Dvir, Croot–Lev–Pach) for existence over F_p
connection: Polynomial method proves existence/size bounds pointwise at each q ↔ ES has a fibre over F_p? (local solvability is trivial).
why: The polynomial method proves things at every prime with no averaging; a polynomial-method argument would need a finite-field shadow of 'integral positive' certificates.
first_step: Find a finite-field statement (over F_p) whose truth implies ES(p) — e.g. 'a certain set S ⊂ F_p² of size ≫ p contains a point of a curve' — and test if the polynomial method applies.

title: Combinatorial Nullstellensatz: ES certificate as nonvanishing of a coefficient
connection: Alon's CN: if a monomial coefficient is nonzero, a nonvanishing point exists in a grid ↔ ES certificates as a grid point avoiding a hypersurface.
why: Repo lists Alon CN in deep-lane catalogue; a specific construction with explicit coefficient computation is the missing piece.
first_step: Write a polynomial over F_ℓ (ℓ auxiliary) on the grid of (u,C) ≤ log p whose nonvanishing implies (4uC−1) | p+u; compute the leading coefficient symbolically.

title: Chevalley–Warning parity: number of solutions mod ℓ of a polynomial system
connection: CW gives #solutions ≡ 0 mod p for low-degree systems ↔ ES certificate count parity.
why: If a set of size ≡ 1 mod 2 can be shown to inject into ES certificates, existence follows (parity trick).
first_step: Find a polynomial system over F_2 or F_3 whose solution set maps onto ES(p) certificates for p ≤ 10³; check CW degree condition.

title: Grothendieck–Lefschetz trace: counting F_q-points of the ES surface with p-adic shadow
connection: #U_n(F_q) given by cohomology traces ↔ integral point existence is not a point count, but mod-q counts of the 'certificate variety' (with tied modulus) could vary with q in a structured way.
why: If the certificate variety V_p has an ℓ-adic cohomology computable as a function of p, Lefschetz numbers might encode R(p) mod something.
first_step: Count F_q points of {(u,B,C): 4uBC − u − B = p} for small q, p and see the dependence on (p mod q) — compare with genus/BM layer.

title: Motivic / Grothendieck ring class of the certificate variety
connection: Class of {4uBC − u − B = n} in K₀(Var) ↔ point counts over all finite fields at once.
why: Cheap structural fact; might show the certificate variety is stably rational, giving parametrisations.
first_step: Compute: for fixed n, the variety 4uBC − u − B = n is a smooth affine threefold; determine its class and rationality (solve for C when 4uB ≠ 0: rational).

title: Hyperbolic lattice-point counting with congruence: Selberg–Kuznetsov and the SL₂ form
connection: SL₂ form: matrices [[a,p],[c,d]] with c ∈ 4ℕ, a ≡ d ≡ −1 mod c ↔ counting lattice points of Γ in a region with fixed top-right entry p.
why: Fixed-entry counting in SL₂(ℤ) is a 'one-sided' problem: the set of matrices with b = p is a coset of a unipotent group; spectral methods give asymptotics in |p| with error p^θ — too big, but the structure is clean.
first_step: Formulate R(p) as Σ_{γ ∈ U\Γ/…} with b-entry p and congruence; compute its spectral expansion's main term and check it equals M₀.

title: Expander graphs: Cayley graph of SL₂(ℤ/q) with ES generators
connection: Bourgain–Gamburd expansion ↔ SL₂ word forms of ES; certificates are short words landing in a coset.
why: Short-word existence in expanders is guaranteed only for word length ≥ log q; ES words have length 3 (fixed) — but generators vary with p. Explore alphabets that grow with p.
first_step: For q = small modulus, compute the fraction of SL₂(ℤ/q) hit by ES₅ words with entries ≤ p and compare with random.

title: Apollonian packings: Ford circles of 4/p and three tangent circles
connection: Descartes curvatures and Egyptian fractions: Ford circles at a/b have curvature 2b² ↔ 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z as a curvature relation?
why: Apollonian local-global (with reciprocity obstructions, HKRS) is the closest 'thin orbit' analogue; a literal geometric embedding of ES into a circle packing would let one import RS/HKRS results.
first_step: Search for a circle configuration whose curvatures are (x,y,z,p) related by 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p (inversion of Descartes-type relations).

title: Stern–Brocot / Calkin–Wilf tree paths of 4/p
connection: 4/p's position in the Stern–Brocot tree is encoded by its CF ↔ ES₅ continued-fraction length condition.
why: Tree-path combinatorics (run-length encoding) gives a visual/automaton description of when short Egyptian decompositions exist.
first_step: Compute SB paths of 4/p and of (4x−p)/(px) for successful x; look for a pattern in path run-lengths.

title: Farey graph geodesics and ES as a 'triangle' in the Farey tessellation
connection: 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p ↔ mediants/Farey neighbours: Egyptian splitting a/b = 1/x + c/d occurs along Farey edges.
why: Hyperbolic geometry of the Farey graph might turn ES into a bounded-length path existence between two cusps — geometric group theory tools (Gromov hyperbolicity) apply.
first_step: Express each ES solution as a path in the Farey graph from 4/p to 0 and record lengths/turn sequences for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Geodesic flow on the modular surface and closed geodesics of discriminant tied to p
connection: Closed geodesics correspond to real quadratic forms; ES certificates might correspond to geodesics passing through a cusp neighbourhood.
why: Equidistribution of closed geodesics (Duke) holds for each large discriminant pointwise — a rare pointwise equidistribution theorem.
first_step: Identify a discriminant D(p) and a target set in the unit tangent bundle such that 'some geodesic of discriminant D(p) visits the set' ⟹ ES(p); check if target set size is ≫ D^{-δ}.

title: Lattice reduction geometry: ES as short vector in a p-dependent lattice of bounded dimension
connection: Repo has lattices L_ρ; Minkowski's theorem gives short vectors pointwise ↔ need vector in a prescribed coset/positive cone.
why: Minkowski is pointwise (T-type size squeeze); the question is whether some lattice of determinant ≍ p has a short vector that is automatically a certificate.
first_step: List repo lattice forms; for each compute Minkowski's guaranteed short vector length vs certificate size bound.

title: Thue's lemma / pigeonhole for x ≡ ay mod p with small x, y and ES
connection: Thue: for any a there exist |x|,|y| ≤ √p with x ≡ ay (mod p) ↔ ES Type II pair form p ≡ −(u+B) mod 4uB.
why: Thue is the prototypical pointwise size-squeeze; Fermat two squares follows. Is there a Thue-type statement with a modulus depending on the variables?
first_step: Search for a fixed modulus M(p) and a residue a(p) such that a small solution of x ≡ a·y mod M yields an ES certificate; test numerically for p ≤ 10⁴.

title: Pell equations and ES: x² − D y² = ±4p via units
connection: Representations of 4p or p by norm forms of real quadratic fields always exist when the class group is trivial ↔ ES certificates as norms.
why: Norm-form existence is pointwise (class field theory: p splits ⟹ represented by some form in class group). ES would need a norm-form whose class group is trivial and whose representation yields a certificate.
first_step: Look for D (fixed, small) with h(D) = 1 such that every representation p = N(α) produces an ES certificate via an explicit formula; test D = 5, 8, 12, 13.

title: Class field theory: ES(p) ⇐ p splits completely in some field K_p of bounded degree?
connection: If ES(p) held whenever p splits in a fixed field K, Chebotarev would give density; ES needs every p, so need a family of fields covering all splitting types.
why: Mordell's identities are of exactly this type (residue classes = splitting in cyclotomic fields). ES's hard classes are 'split completely in ℚ(ζ_840)' — need non-abelian fields.
first_step: Check: are ES-easy primes (with tiny certificates) characterised by splitting in a non-abelian field (e.g. x³ − x − 1)? Compute splitting behaviour correlation for p ≡ 1 mod 840.

title: Non-abelian identities: polynomial certificates valid on primes split in a non-abelian extension
connection: Mordell–Schinzel forbids polynomial identities on residue classes; but identities valid when p = f(t) for a polynomial f (thin sets) or when p splits in a non-abelian field are not excluded.
why: Non-abelian splitting conditions are not residue classes, so they evade the Mordell–Schinzel obstruction; a finite cover of all primes by non-abelian conditions is impossible (Chebotarev), but combinations may help.
first_step: For p ≡ 1 mod 840, test whether p = N(α) for α in ℤ[ζ_3, 2^{1/3}] (i.e. p = x³-form represented) gives a uniform certificate formula.

title: Binary cubic forms: Delone–Faddeev and ES certificates as cubic rings
connection: Binary cubic forms ↔ cubic rings; 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is a ternary cubic, but its slices are binary cubics.
why: Bhargava-style parametrisation might identify ES solutions with ideal classes in cubic rings of discriminant tied to n; existence via class group nontriviality?
first_step: Compute the binary cubic obtained by fixing z in 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) and its discriminant as function of n,z.

title: Bhargava cubes / higher composition laws for the trilinear form xyz
connection: The equation is a symmetric trilinear/cubic form ↔ Bhargava's cubes (2×2×2 integer cubes) parametrise triples of binary quadratic forms.
why: Tripling structure (x,y,z symmetric) may correspond to a composition law: ES(p) ⟺ some triple of forms composes to a specified class.
first_step: Write 4xyz − n(xy+yz+zx) as hyperdeterminant-like expression and check whether it equals Cayley's hyperdeterminant of some cube with entries linear in (x,y,z,n).

title: Elliptic curve E_n: y² = x³ + … attached to 4/n and its rank
connection: Repo has 'ec' data; 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n with a fixed ratio gives elliptic curves ↔ positivity of rank / torsion structure.
why: If some explicit elliptic curve over ℚ attached to p has a rational point that yields a certificate whenever its rank ≥ 1, BSD-parity (root number) could force existence for half the primes.
first_step: Inspect data/ec in repo; check whether root number of the associated curve correlates with certificate existence at small size.

title: Root number parity forcing: Dokchitser-style 'rank is odd ⟹ point exists' for a certificate curve
connection: If ES(p) ⇐ E_p(ℚ) has a point of a certain type and w(E_p) = −1 for all relevant p, parity conjecture would force rank ≥ 1.
why: Parity forcing is a genuinely pointwise existence source (R-type, conditional on finiteness of Sha or parity conjecture).
first_step: Search for a family of elliptic curves E_p over ℚ indexed by p with w(E_p) = −1 for every p ≡ 1 mod 24 and with points that map to ES solutions.

title: Heegner points: an algebraic point forced to exist for each p
connection: Heegner points on X₀(N) exist for every imaginary quadratic field satisfying Heegner hypothesis ↔ ES certificate = a forced algebraic object at p.
why: Heegner points exist pointwise by construction (CM theory); they are the archetype of R-type existence. Mapping one to an integer solution would need a 'positivity' extraction.
first_step: Ask: does the CM point of discriminant −4p (or −p) on X₀(4) have any coordinate whose norm relates to 4Cp+1-type integers?

title: Gross–Zagier singular moduli factorisation as divisor-structure input
connection: Norms of differences of singular moduli have explicitly known prime factorisations (all primes ≤ D1D2/4) ↔ ES needs divisors of p-tied integers in a class.
why: An integer tied to p with explicitly controlled factorisation (only small primes, with Legendre-symbol constraints) is exactly what the 'class gate' wants.
first_step: Compute N(j(τ_{−4p}) − j(τ_{−3}))-type quantities for small p and check if they produce divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of 4Cp+1-type integers.

title: Lehmer/Lucas sequences: primitive divisors of u_n tied to p
connection: Bilu–Hanrot–Voutier: Lucas sequences have primitive divisors for n > 30 ↔ existence of a prime ≡ ±1 mod n dividing u_n (forced class!).
why: Primitive divisors of Φ_n-type values lie in ≡ ±1 mod n classes automatically — a rigid source of divisors in a tied residue class (the ES gate wants d ≡ −1 mod 4C).
first_step: Find a Lucas sequence u_m(p) with index m ~ 4C such that p-tied integers 4Cp+1 contain u_m's primitive divisor; test small cases.

title: Cyclotomic polynomial values Φ_m(a) have prime factors ≡ 1 mod m: tie 4C to m
connection: Every prime factor of Φ_m(a) not dividing m is ≡ 1 mod m ↔ ES needs a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C (so 'Φ' for −1 class: factors of a^{m}+1-type numbers ≡ 1 mod 2m).
why: A divisor ≡ −1 mod c is different from ≡ 1; products of two factors ≡ −1 … Need a construction where an integer automatically has a divisor ≡ −1 mod c: e.g. Φ_m(a)-like numbers N with N ≡ −1 mod c themselves.
first_step: Search for algebraic identities 4Cp + 1 = A·B with A ≡ −1 mod 4C forced by cyclotomic structure when p has a special form (p = Φ_m(t)?).

title: Sophie Germain / Aurifeuillean factorisation families extended to primes p of special shape
connection: Repo proved thin families via algebraic factorisations (4X⁴+1) ↔ Aurifeuillean factorisations of Φ_n(x) at special x.
why: Every Aurifeuillean identity gives an infinite family where a p-tied integer factors algebraically; systematically enumerating them could produce more proved thin families.
first_step: List Aurifeuillean identities (Brent's tables) and test each for producing an ES certificate on a polynomial family of n.

title: Abc conjecture consequences for ES failures
connection: ABC controls radicals ↔ an ES counterexample p forces all 4Cp+1 (C ≤ polylog) to avoid divisors in −1 mod 4C; does that force smoothness/radical patterns contradicting abc?
why: Implications from abc to Diophantine non-existence are standard; here we want abc ⟹ existence, which is unusual but possible via 'no huge prime-power structure' arguments.
first_step: Check whether the failure of (★) for p forces 4Cp+1 to be prime or a prime power for many C — and whether that's restricted by known results (it isn't by abc; record negative).

title: Bunyakovsky/Schinzel H ⟹ infinitely many ES-hard-for-small-menu primes (sanity: unconditional disproof shapes)
connection: Under Schinzel H, for any finite menu of certificate types there are infinitely many p evading it ↔ B1 barrier.
why: This is known (B1). Including as calibration of any proposed proof: it must use an unbounded menu.
first_step: Already in repo (B1); first step: check that every item in this list proposes an unbounded menu or flags otherwise.

title: Galois representations: the Tate module of the certificate variety's Jacobian-like object
connection: If R(p) = trace of Frobenius on some motive (minus main term), Weil bounds give pointwise control ↔ but R(p) is integral-point count, not F_p count.
why: Integral-point counts are not traces; yet the e-slice form counts divisors mod e — a character sum over (ℤ/e)^× which is a trace on a finite group algebra.
first_step: Write R(p) = Σ_e Σ_χ mod e χ(−1)·(Σ_{ab|N_e} χ(a b̄)) / φ(e) and see if the inner sum is a trace of something with Deligne-type bounds.

title: Arakelov / heights: ES certificate size as a height and slopes of an arithmetic bundle
connection: Minimal certificate size vs p ↔ successive minima of an Arakelov vector bundle attached to p (Bost's slopes).
why: Slope inequalities give existence of small sections pointwise (Siegel lemma); ES needs a 'section' landing in an integrality cone.
first_step: Model the (u,C) search space as a hermitian ℤ-module and compute slopes for p ≤ 10⁴; compare with minimal certificate heights.

title: Siegel's lemma with congruence conditions: a small solution of a linear system tied to p
connection: Siegel's lemma guarantees small integer solutions of underdetermined linear systems ↔ ES Type II linear in C for fixed (u,B).
why: For fixed u, the condition (4uC−1) | p+u is linear in a hidden quotient: p + u = k(4uC − 1); i.e. p = 4uCk − u − k: symmetric bilinear in (C,k)! Siegel can't force bilinear, but the structure is a 'multiplicative Siegel lemma'.
first_step: Note p + u + k = 4uCk: for fixed u, need p ≡ −u − k mod 4uk with C integer. Tabulate minimal u per p and the 'free' parameter k distribution.

title: R(p) as a partition function: Z(β) = Σ over trial pairs of exp(−β·cost) and the β→∞ limit
connection: Statistical mechanics: count of certificates = zero-temperature limit of a partition function over the trial set 𝓡 with energy = 'distance from divisibility' ↔ R(p).
why: Smooth relaxations (finite β) are analytically tractable (sums of exponentials of residues) and could be bounded below; the question is whether a β-interpolation lower bound survives β → ∞.
first_step: Define E(u,C) = ((p+u) mod (4uC−1))/(4uC−1) and compute Z(β) = Σ e^{−βE} for p ≤ 10⁵; check monotone behaviour of log Z(β) vs log R(p) at large β.

title: Random energy model (Derrida) as null model for certificate counts
connection: REM: 2^N independent energies; ground-state statistics ↔ R(p) as count of ≍ p log p rare independent-ish events with polylog mean.
why: REM predicts Poisson zero probability exp(−mean); calibrating ES's zero probability against REM vs correlated models (GREM) quantifies 'how independent' the events are.
first_step: Fit the empirical distribution of R(p)/M(p) over primes ≤ 10⁸ to Poisson vs negative-binomial vs log-normal; report best-fit dispersion.

title: Cramér-type random model for ES: predicted number of counterexamples
connection: Model each trial event (4uC−1) | p+u as independent with probability 1/(4uC−1) ↔ expected failures Σ_p exp(−c log² p) < ∞.
why: Gives a quantitative 'ES is true with overwhelming probability' heuristic; repo has (J)97 zero law. Recompute with correct dependence structure (pair complementarity, genus layer).
first_step: Re-derive P(R(p)=0) under a model respecting R(p) even-ness and the BM character; compare with observed (★)-line failure counts.

title: Large deviations: rate function for lower tail of R(p)
connection: Lower tail P(R(p) ≤ εM) in a random model ↔ Janson inequality for sums of dependent indicators.
why: Janson's inequality gives exp(−μ²/(2Δ)) bounds; computing Δ (pair correlation of certificate events) explicitly for ES yields a falsifiable heuristic and identifies dangerous correlations.
first_step: Compute Δ = Σ_{i~j} P(A_i ∧ A_j) for ES certificate events empirically (pairs of (u,C) sharing a modulus factor) at p ~ 10⁷.

title: Lovász Local Lemma inverted: certificate events as a dependency graph, and 'all fail' probability
connection: LLL gives positive probability that no bad event occurs ↔ we want the opposite: probability all certificate events fail is small; Shearer's bound on the independence polynomial.
why: Independence-polynomial (hard-core gas) view gives exact formulas for 'all fail' in a dependency model; maps ES to a lattice-gas zero question.
first_step: Build the dependency graph of certificate events (shared prime factors of moduli) for p ≤ 10⁴ and compute the independence polynomial evaluation as a model zero-probability.

title: Lee–Yang zeros of a certificate generating polynomial
connection: Lee–Yang: zeros of partition functions on the unit circle ↔ define P_p(z) = Σ_{certificates} z^{size}; zero locations might obey a circle theorem that forces P_p(1) > 0.
why: Circle theorems give positivity from algebraic structure (R-type). Need a polynomial whose evaluation at 1 counts certificates and whose zeros are provably off z=1.
first_step: Construct P_p(z) = Σ_{(u,B,C) certificate} z^{u+B+C} for small p and plot zeros; look for regularities.

title: Random matrix statistics of the sequence R(p)/M(p)
connection: Fluctuations of arithmetic counts often match RMT (e.g. L-function zeros) ↔ R(p) normalised.
why: If fluctuations are Gaussian with variance ~ (log p)^a, the lower tail model sharpens; RMT mismatch indicates hidden structure.
first_step: Compute variance of R(p) − M_BM(p) in windows and its scaling with log p for p ≤ 10⁸ (repo data).

title: Spectral form factor / pair correlation of 'certificate moduli' 4uC−1 dividing p+u
connection: Quantum chaos tools on number-theoretic sequences ↔ distribution of the set of successful (u,C) per p.
why: Clustering/repulsion of certificates would indicate dependencies affecting zero probability.
first_step: For each p compute the set of successful (u,C); measure nearest-neighbour spacing distribution in log-scale over p ≤ 10⁶.

title: Percolation on the divisor graph: does p 'percolate' to a certificate?
connection: Divisor-lattice percolation ↔ ES certificate as a connection path in a graph whose nodes are p-tied integers and edges are divisibility in classes.
why: Percolation has sharp threshold theorems (Friedgut–Kalai); a giant-component argument could give existence when density exceeds a threshold.
first_step: Define graph G_p on {4Cp+1 : C ≤ T} ∪ divisors with edges by residue condition; compute component sizes for hard vs easy p.

title: Kinetic/flow interpretation: Euclid algorithm as a dynamical system and ES as short-orbit condition
connection: Gauss map dynamics on rationals ↔ ES₅ continued fraction length ≤ 3 for a p-tied rational.
why: Hensley/Baladi–Vallée transfer operators give distribution of CF lengths of rationals with denominator p; ES asks for one rational in a family with short length.
first_step: Use Baladi–Vallée style counting: number of a/p with CF length ≤ 3 and partial quotient constraints; compare with ES₅ counts.

title: Transfer-matrix method for counting certificate words
connection: Count words tuv − u − v = p via a transfer matrix over residues ↔ ES₅/I3 words.
why: Transfer matrices make counting mod q exact and expose eigenvalue gaps; might give the main term and fluctuations as eigenvalue contributions.
first_step: Build the mod-q transfer matrix for words (t,u,v) with tuv − u − v ≡ p mod q and compute its spectrum for q ≤ 50.

title: Integrable systems: Somos sequences / QRT maps preserving 1/x+1/y+1/z
connection: QRT maps and Somos recurrences preserve rational invariants ↔ an integrable map on (x,y,z) preserving 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/n would generate solutions from one.
why: A birational map preserving the ES surface with integer-preserving (Laurent) property gives infinite families of solutions from a seed — a group action (Markoff-like).
first_step: Search for birational involutions of the ES surface of the form z ↦ (rational in x,y)/z (Vieta for the quadratic in z after clearing denominators) and test integrality.

title: Vieta jumping on the ES surface: z appears linearly, but 4xyz − nxy − nxz − nyz is bilinear in (y,z)
connection: Vieta jumping needs quadratic in one variable; ES is bilinear ↔ after substitution (e.g. y = x + s) a quadratic may appear.
why: Vieta jumping solved IMO 1988/6 (a²+b²)/(ab+1) pointwise via descent; an ES descent would be an R-type extraction.
first_step: Try substitutions y = x + s, z = x + t and look for an equation quadratic in x with integral Vieta partner.

title: Sandpile / chip-firing model on a graph attached to p
connection: Abelian sandpile groups are finite abelian groups (Jacobians of graphs) ↔ (ℤ/4C)^× targets; chip-firing gives combinatorial certificates of group elements.
why: Repo has bsA_selling_sandpile; a chip-firing reachability formulation of 'divisor in class −1' could import graph-theoretic tools.
first_step: Read BRAINSTORM/bsA_selling_sandpile.md and extract its open step; try one graph family (cycle with chords) parametrised by p.

title: Ising-like spin model: the BM character as a spin and T(p) as magnetisation
connection: T(p) = Σ (−uB/p)/φ(4uB) is a weighted sum of ±1 spins over pairs ↔ magnetisation of a spin system with couplings from multiplicativity.
why: Spin-glass bounds or correlation inequalities (Griffiths/GKS) give pointwise inequalities for ferromagnetic systems; multiplicativity (−uB/p) = (−u/p)(B/p) is a product spin structure (Mattis model).
first_step: Write T(p) = Σ_{u,B} s_u s'_B w(u,B) with s_u = (u/p): it's a Mattis-type bilinear form; compute the max over arbitrary sign patterns vs actual to see how far from worst case.

title: Free probability / random multiplicative functions: replace (·/p) by random ±1 multiplicative f
connection: Random multiplicative function models (Harper) ↔ T(p) with Legendre symbol replaced by Steinhaus/Rademacher multiplicative f.
why: Harper's 'better than square-root cancellation' for random multiplicative sums suggests T(p) behaves better than worst case; quantifies M_BM lower bound tightness.
first_step: Simulate T_f = Σ f(u)f(B)·(−1-twist)/φ(4uB) for random multiplicative f and compare distribution to empirical T(p).

title: Brownian / random-walk model for the greedy remainder chain
connection: Successive remainders in Egyptian expansions as a Markov chain ↔ probability the chain hits numerator 1 at step 2.
why: Gives a heuristic per-p probability that simple algorithms succeed; separates algorithmic from existential difficulty.
first_step: Simulate the 'first-term then remainder' chain over all first terms x ∈ [p/4, 3p/4] and record the success probability distribution per p.

title: Renormalisation group heuristic: coarse-graining p by its residue mod growing moduli
connection: RG flows of residue-class statistics ↔ Mordell → 840 → larger moduli filters; each scale removes a fraction of primes.
why: If the fraction surviving filters at modulus M decays like 1/(log M)^a, an RG fixed point analysis predicts how many filters are needed for primes ≤ X.
first_step: Using verification-style filters, measure fraction of primes surviving modulus-M filters for M in a geometric sequence; fit decay exponent.

title: Entropy/information-theoretic view: bits of p needed to specify a certificate
connection: A certificate (u,B,C) has ~3 log log p bits beyond p ↔ information about p revealed by existence of a certificate.
why: If certificate existence for p were 'hard information', compression arguments (Kolmogorov) could say something; at least clarifies that certificates are tiny relative to p.
first_step: Compute the empirical entropy of the minimal certificate (u,C) distribution conditioned on p mod small moduli; does p mod 840·k predict it?

title: Kolmogorov complexity argument: a counterexample p would be 'simple'?
connection: Incompressibility method: if every p ≤ X of high complexity has a certificate, counterexamples must be low-complexity ↔ disproof search direction.
why: Adversarial searches already target structured p; formalising 'low complexity' (short description) to prioritise searches is a meta improvement.
first_step: Rank candidate primes by description length (e.g. p = a·b^k + c with small a,b,c) and search ES hardness there first.

title: Ergodic theory of multiplicative semigroups: Furstenberg ×2×3 and certificates as orbit points
connection: Furstenberg's ×2×3 rigidity ↔ the multiplicative semigroup of divisors of p-tied integers acting on (ℤ/4C)^×.
why: Rigidity theorems give pointwise density of orbits (every infinite ×2×3-invariant closed set is everything); a finite analogue (Bourgain–Lindenstrauss–Michel–Venkatesh effective) gives 'orbits of 2,3 in (ℤ/q)^× are dense'.
first_step: Check BLMV/Bourgain effective ×a×b results: does {2^i 3^j mod q} hit −1 for all q with small exponents? Then ask if 4Cp+1-divisors contain a fixed multiplicative structure.

title: Mixing of the map p ↦ (p mod 4uC−1) as u,C vary: equidistribution of residues of a single integer
connection: Residues of a fixed p modulo a growing family of moduli ↔ ES needs p ≡ −u mod (4uC−1) for some pair; this is 'one integer vs many moduli' — Erdős–Turán type discrepancy.
why: Discrepancy of {p/m} for m in a structured set is a classic (Vinogradov-type) problem; known results (e.g. on p mod m for m ≤ √p) might give existence in some ranges.
first_step: Measure discrepancy of fractional parts {(p+u)/(4uC−1)} over the trial set and compare with random; the ES event is the fractional part being exactly 0.

title: Billiards / circle rotation: p mod m for consecutive m as a rotation-like sequence
connection: p mod m for m near √p behaves like a quadratic sequence (Dirichlet divisor problem) ↔ ES divisibility events are zeros of p mod (4uC − 1).
why: Near m ≈ √p, p mod m follows parabolic arcs; divisors appear at structured places. Could the ES moduli family hit such arcs?
first_step: Plot (m, (p+u) mod m) for moduli m = 4uC−1 near √p and look for parabolic patterns permitting a forced zero.

title: Quantum unique ergodicity analogy: certificates as 'mass' of a p-dependent state
connection: QUE for Hecke eigenforms gives pointwise equidistribution in the eigenvalue aspect ↔ ES certificate counts as 'mass in a small set'.
why: QUE is pointwise in the spectral parameter (Lindenstrauss, Soundararajan); a QUE-type statement for a p-indexed family would give pointwise counts, but the target set must be fixed-size.
first_step: Find whether R(p)/M(p) can be written as ⟨φ_p, 1_A φ_p⟩ for some natural p-family of states φ_p and fixed set A.

title: Thermodynamic formalism for Egyptian fraction expansions (Engel/Sylvester series dynamics)
connection: Engel expansions and Sylvester series have ergodic theory (Rényi) ↔ 3-term Egyptian representations as short orbits.
why: Known metric theory of Engel/Sylvester digits could supply heuristic densities for 'expansions of length 3'.
first_step: Compute the Engel/Sylvester (greedy) expansion of 4/p and its length distribution over primes; correlate with ES difficulty.

title: Phase transition in random Egyptian-fraction CSPs (k-term with bounded denominators)
connection: Random CSP satisfiability thresholds ↔ ES as satisfiability of a sparse constraint system indexed by p.
why: If ES-like random instances undergo a sharp transition at 'expected solutions ≈ 1', ES sits at expected ≈ log² p — deep in the satisfiable phase; how deep quantifies safety margin.
first_step: Define random analogues: replace p by random integers in a residue class and compute the fraction with zero solutions as function of bound on denominators.

title: Benford/scale invariance of minimal certificate sizes
connection: Distribution of the leading digits / log-size of minimal certificates ↔ scale-invariance tests detect hidden multiplicative structure.
why: Cheap statistical fingerprint; deviations indicate structure worth explaining.
first_step: Compute log(min y/p) distribution over primes ≤ 10⁸ and test for scale invariance.

title: Extreme value theory for max over p ≤ X of (minimal certificate size)
connection: Gumbel/Fréchet laws for maxima of iid ↔ max_p min-certificate as function of X.
why: If the max grows like (log X)^a with EVT-consistent fluctuations, extrapolate beyond 10¹⁸; deviations flag structure.
first_step: From repo census data, extract record-setting primes for 'least u in I3 word' and fit EVT growth.

title: Records sequence of hardest primes as an OEIS-style object
connection: Sequence of primes p where min certificate size exceeds all previous ↔ OEIS has such records for ES? (check).
why: Records concentrate structure (adversarial primes); their pattern (residues, factorisations of p±small) suggests failure mechanisms.
first_step: Search OEIS for 'Erdos-Straus' sequences; compute records for 'smallest x in 4/p = 1/x+…' and submit/compare.

title: Fokker–Planck / diffusion model of log R(p) along p
connection: log R(p) as a stochastic process in p ↔ smooth main term plus noise.
why: Autocorrelation of R across nearby primes (p, p+840k) shows whether difficulty is local in residue or random.
first_step: Compute autocorrelation of R(p)/M(p) between primes in the same class mod 840 with lag k.

title: Maximum entropy model for certificate distribution given residue constraints
connection: MaxEnt with constraints p mod q for q ≤ Q ↔ best prediction of R(p) from local data.
why: The gap between MaxEnt prediction and actual R(p) is the 'global' part; if it's small, ES difficulty is local-plus-noise.
first_step: Fit log R(p) ~ Σ_q β_q·1[p ≡ a mod q] by regularised regression and report R² vs Q.

title: Boltzmann sampling of certificates for very large p (10^100)
connection: Analytic combinatorics Boltzmann samplers ↔ draw random (u,C) weighted by 1/(4uC−1) and test divisibility.
why: Monte Carlo estimates of R(p) at astronomical p (where full enumeration is impossible) test whether the main term persists; finds adversarial p faster.
first_step: Implement weighted sampling over (u,C) for p ~ 10^50 random primes ≡ 1 mod 840 and estimate hits per 10⁹ samples vs M(p) prediction.

title: Physics of Egyptian fractions: resistor networks (parallel resistances add reciprocally)
connection: Parallel resistors: 1/R = Σ 1/R_i ↔ ES: can resistance p/4 be made from three integer resistors in parallel.
why: Recasts ES in electrical-network language; series-parallel networks and their combinatorics (e.g. counting resistances achievable with n unit resistors) might suggest generalisations (network with 3 components + series).
first_step: Formulate 'p/4 Ω from three integer-Ω resistors in parallel' and a relaxation allowing one series connection; count solutions of the relaxation.

title: Optics / lens equation 1/f = 1/u + 1/v as a 2-term analogue and thin-lens compound systems
connection: Thin-lens combination 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2 + 1/f3 ↔ ES as three thin lenses in contact with focal length p/4.
why: Pedagogical; might attract physics-community recreational solvers. Not a proof tool.
first_step: Write a short outreach note 'three lenses for every prime' for recreational audiences (cheap community lever).

title: Harmonic-mean interpretation: p/4·3 is the harmonic mean of x,y,z
connection: 4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z ⟺ harmonic mean H(x,y,z) = 3p/4 ↔ means inequalities (H ≤ G ≤ A) give box constraints.
why: Box constraints from mean inequalities are already used; the 'harmonic mean of three integers equals 3p/4' phrasing might connect to integer means literature.
first_step: Search 'integers with prescribed harmonic mean' literature for existence theorems.

title: Crystallography / Bravais lattices: 1/x+1/y+1/z as Miller-index relation
connection: Miller-index plane equations x/a + y/b + z/c = 1 ↔ the plane through (x,0,0),(0,y,0),(0,0,z) contains the point (p/4,p/4,p/4) ⟺ 1/x+1/y+1/z = 4/p.
why: Geometric reformulation: ES(p) ⟺ some lattice plane with positive integer axis intercepts passes through (p/4)(1,1,1). Lattice-plane counting (geometry of numbers) might apply.
first_step: Use this: count lattice planes through q = (p/4)(1,1,1) with integer intercepts; relate to primitive vectors (1/x,1/y,1/z) scaled — check if this is a known equivalence to ET.

title: Intercept form: ES as a plane through the diagonal point — projective dual
connection: Dual: points (1/x,1/y,1/z) of the plane X+Y+Z = 4/p with unit-fraction coordinates ↔ rational points on a plane with all coordinates reciprocals of integers.
why: Duality may bring Schmidt subspace theorem-type tools (points of small height on planes with coordinates of special form).
first_step: Record the dual formulation and check whether Schmidt-subspace-type results bound the number of solutions in a way that conflicts with zero (no: they give upper bounds) — note as calibration.

title: Mechanical analogy: springs in series (compliance adds) and integer stiffness
connection: Springs in series: 1/k = Σ 1/k_i ↔ same algebra as resistors; equivalent reformulation.
why: Duplicate of resistor item in algebra but different community (mechanics puzzles); keep as outreach variant.
first_step: Combine with resistor outreach note (no separate work).

title: Kinetic theory of the 'trial division' process: occupancy problem
connection: Balls-in-bins: each trial modulus m 'catches' p if p ≡ r_m mod m ↔ ES is non-empty-catch.
why: Occupancy problems with heterogeneous bin probabilities have sharp zero-probability estimates (Poisson clumping heuristic, Aldous).
first_step: Apply Aldous' Poisson clumping heuristic to ES with clumps = shared-factor moduli; compute adjusted zero probability.

title: Stein–Chen method: total variation distance of R(p)/2 to Poisson
connection: Stein–Chen bounds Poisson approximation for sums of weakly dependent indicators ↔ R(p) half-count.
